definition: A closed region of allowed combined accelerations, by duration, that a ride must stay inside.
A pressure tank where hydraulic fluid compresses nitrogen gas to store launch energy.
The noise exposure, 85 dBA averaged over eight hours in US rules, above which hearing protection and monitoring are required.
A pneumatic, hydraulic or electric device that turns a control signal into one movement of a figure or set piece.
Janet Murray's term for the satisfying power to take meaningful action and see its results.
A crowd model in which each simulated guest follows its own simple rules, so group behavior emerges from many individuals.
A thin, dark, translucent coat of paint that settles into recesses to make a new surface look old and dirty.
The floating feeling near zero g when the track drops away faster than gravity pulls the rider.
A long, seamless recording of environmental sound such as birds, wind or distant machinery that plays continuously in a space.
Storyboards or simple 3D shots cut to a soundtrack so the team can feel the pacing of a ride.
Measured body dimensions from population surveys, used to size seats, restraints and reach limits.
A pivoting pawl under the car that drops into a ratchet so the train can climb but never slide back.
The looped background music a land plays to set its mood, usually without lyrics so it never competes with speech.
The welded steel skeleton that gives rockwork or a figure its shape before any surface goes on.
The person who guards the look of a project from first sketch to final paint on site.
A royalty-free protocol from Artistic Licence that carries DMX512 and RDM data over Ethernet.
The ASTM International committee, formed in 1978, that writes the main North American amusement ride standards.
Kotler's term for deliberately designing the sensory qualities of a space to produce a wanted response in visitors.
Kaplan's theory that softly fascinating natural scenes let the tired, effortful kind of attention recover.
The chosen blend of thrill, family, kiddie and show content so every guest type stays busy all day.
A benchmark of how many attractions a guest should be able to experience per hour, used to size the attraction mix.
Sound from one themed zone leaking into a neighbouring zone where it breaks the theme.
Disney's trademark for figures that move and speak in sync with recorded audio, first shown in 1963.
A see-through head-mounted display that overlays characters and targets onto real sets, as on Mario Kart: Bowser's Challenge.
The share of scheduled operating time during which a ride is actually open to guests.
An emotion triggered by vastness that forces you to update how you see the world.
Service areas hidden from guests: docks, plant rooms, wardrobe, break rooms and roads.
What happened in a place before the guest arrived, usually implied by details rather than told.
Deciding not to join a queue because it looks too long.
The capacity measure for a water park: how many people can safely be in the water and on the decks at once.
Disney's small bipedal robot character, revealed in 2023 and roaming daily at Disneyland's Galaxy's Edge from April 2024.
A numbered list of a ride's moments with what guests see, feel and learn at each one.
The raised, planted earth wall around a park that hides the outside world from guests.
Building information modelling: one shared 3D model that carries geometry plus data for every discipline.
Our innate pull toward living things and natural settings, which planting and water in parks quietly satisfy.
A lamp that emits mostly long-wave ultraviolet light, making fluorescent paint glow while the room stays dark.
A section of track with its own stop and start control; only one train may occupy it.
Control logic that divides a track into sections and never lets two trains occupy the same one.
The plan for where performers or figures stand and move so the audience can see the action.
The first idea stage where cost and practicality are set aside so the boldest concepts can surface.
A stretch of track with brakes that slows or stops a train, usually before the station.
Money spent on long-lived assets such as new rides, lands and hotels, as opposed to daily running costs.
The share of people in a market area expected to visit a park in a year.
A sled running between the rails that hooks a train and tows it during a hydraulic or pneumatic launch.
The tall landmark at the heart of a park, such as a castle or mountain, that orients guests and brands the place.
A backstage facility that makes chilled water, hot water and sometimes power for the whole park.
A pivoting hook under the train that catches the lift chain.
A short, intense workshop where client and designers sketch and argue through a concept together.
The way options are arranged and defaulted, which steers decisions without removing any choice.
Software checking where one trade's pipes, steel or scenery collides with another's before construction.
A spiral whose curvature grows in proportion to distance along it, used for loops and transitions.
A teardrop-shaped vertical loop whose tightening curve keeps forces tolerable, used on Revolution in 1976.
The record race for taller and faster coasters that ran roughly from 1989 to 2005.
How easily a scene reads as one organised whole; high coherence lets rich detail feel calm instead of noisy.
A row of small colour thumbnails showing how colour and light change beat by beat through a story or ride.
A Kelvin number describing how warm (orange) or cool (blue) a white light looks; candlelight is low, overcast sky is high.
Paintings and sketches that show what a place will feel like before anyone draws it to scale.
The illustrator who produces the key paintings and sketches that define how an attraction looks and feels.
Continuous measurement of vibration, temperature or pressure on ride components to detect changes from normal.
A category assigned from a seat's accelerations that dictates the type and redundancy of restraint required.
An engineer who programs the PLC and safety logic that moves vehicles between block zones and stops them when sensors disagree.
A reliable pairing between features of different senses, such as high pitch with brightness.
The eyes' slow gain in sensitivity after entering darkness, taking several minutes to approach full.
Ticket prices that vary by calendar date to push demand toward quieter days.
The UK ADIPS certificate issued after pre-use or annual inspection confirming a ride may be operated.
The number of independent ways a platform can move, up to six: surge, sway, heave, roll, pitch and yaw.
Density is people per area; crowding is the unpleasant feeling that there are too many of them, which design can change.
The typical busy day a park is sized for, usually the average of its busiest 15 to 25 days rather than the record day.
The written and drawn record of what the creative team means, which engineers and fabricators must honour.
A worn shortcut created by people repeatedly leaving the official path for a more direct route.
A park that draws guests from across a country or the world for multi-day stays, usually with hotels on site.
A living model of one specific attraction that is kept in step with the real thing by sensor or design data.
Imagineering's Digital Immersive Showroom, a projection room for walking through designs at full scale.
A front-line internship at Walt Disney World for enrolled US college students, a common first step into the industry.
The time between one vehicle leaving the station and the next one leaving.
The 1986 serial lighting-control standard that sends 512 channel values per universe at 250 kbit/s.
How long an experience lasts has little effect on how good or bad it feels in memory.
How many cycles a figure or effect runs per day, which drives wear, inspection and skin replacement.
A park plan that an app rewrites through the day as waits, bookings and a guest's choices change.
A contactless brake in which magnets induce currents in a moving fin, producing drag that rises with speed.
A contactless brake in which fins pass magnets and the induced currents slow the vehicle.
Fading the overlapping edges of neighbouring projectors so several images read as one seamless picture.
A latching red control that brings a ride to a defined safe stop and must be deliberately reset.
The automatic spread of feelings through a group via mimicry of faces, voices and posture.
The European standard for fairground and amusement park rides, split since 2019 into design, operation and inspection parts.
A tracked vehicle with an onboard motion base that adds tilt and bounce, first used on Indiana Jones Adventure.
A planner's tally of hourly capacity across rides, shows and games that a park must provide.
The staged route from car park to first land that moves guests from the real world into the story.
Telling a story through the physical traces left in a space so visitors reconstruct it themselves.
Alterface's term for a trackless dark ride that routes vehicles through rooms in a different order each trip.
A wide view that shows where the story is set, borrowed from film and used at land entrances.
Leftover bodily arousal from one event spilling over and intensifying the feeling of the next.
A short survey interview with guests as they leave the park.
A design whose default state on loss of power or signal is a safe one, such as a spring-applied brake.
Paint and texture applied to a cheap or durable base to make it read as another material, such as aged wood or stone.
An early report that tests whether a project can work on this site, for this market, at this budget.
The animator who authors an animatronic figure's movements and timing against the show's audio and ride cues.
A permanent ride at a park, which in the United States falls outside federal CPSC jurisdiction.
A simulator whose seats are lifted into a dome screen with riders' feet hanging free.
Failure Mode and Effects Analysis, a component-by-component list of how things can fail and what would happen.
Building upper floors or far ends at a smaller scale so a structure looks taller or farther away.
The imagined barrier between performers and audience; role-play cast deliberately break it.
A 3-D curve paired with a moving frame, used to describe a coaster track's position and roll together for optimization.
A dome-shaped screen that fills the viewer's field of view, fed by a fisheye projector or several blended projectors.
The curve relating crowd density to flow, which rises and then collapses as people pack too tightly to move.
The push a seat or restraint gives a rider compared with sitting still, expressed as a multiple of gravity.
A scheduled decision point where a project is approved, sent back or stopped before more money is spent.
Using image or text models, ideally trained on a studio's own archive, to turn a sketch or brief into many candidate concepts.
A pyrotechnic fountain that produces a controlled plume of sparks for a set burn time.
Glass fibre reinforced concrete: thin, light panels used for themed facades and prefabricated rock.
A full-circuit coaster between 300 and 399 ft tall, begun by Millennium Force in 2000.
A family of muted grey-greens Disney paints on fences, show buildings and utilities so the eye slides past them.
A thin metal or glass pattern placed in a spotlight to project a shape such as leaves or a window.
The 1920s boom in wooden coasters that ended with the Great Depression.
Dimming, colourless vision caused by sustained positive g draining blood from the head.
Everything underfoot: paving colour, pattern, texture and scoring, treated as a designed storytelling surface.
The platform position that sorts parties into numbered rows before the gates open.
Technology that produces touch or force sensations, from seat vibration to pneumatic vests, timed to media events.
A crash-test score computed from the head's acceleration over a short window, used to compare coasters with other activities.
Repeated strikes of the head against a hard restraint caused by lateral jolts on a rough ride.
The roll axis chosen to pass through the average rider's chest so that rolls feel nearly force-free.
The seated width across the hips, the measurement that most often decides whether a guest fits a ride seat.
The brake at the lip of a dive coaster's drop that pauses the train face-down before release.
Coating steel by dipping it in molten zinc, which protects as a barrier and sacrificially.
A park layout with one entrance, a central plaza and themed lands radiating out from it.
A coaster with steel track on a mostly wooden structure, such as New Texas Giant.
A launch that fires a train with a cable pulled by hydraulic motors, as on Kingda Ka.
A full-circuit coaster at least 200 ft tall, a class begun by Magnum XL-200 in 1989.
RMC's steel I-beam track that replaces wooden rails on an existing wooden structure.
The International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, the operators' and suppliers' trade body that runs the Expos.
IAAPA's Certified Attractions Professional and Certified Attractions Executive credentials, earned by exam and maintained with continuing education.
Kevin Lynch's term for how easily a place forms a clear mental map in the people who use it.
Walt Disney Imagineering's student design competition, started by Marty Sklar in 1991, with Hong Kong and Shanghai editions.
A Walt Disney Imagineering employee; the company says it spans more than 100 disciplines, not only artists.
The free three-lesson Khan Academy course on theme park design that Disney Imagineering released in 2020.
A mirror facing a half-silvered mirror with lights between them, producing a tunnel of reflections that seems endless.
An organisation registered under a scheme such as ADIPS to review designs and inspect rides independently.
A space syntax measure of how few turns a path is from all others, which predicts how busy it will be.
The museum and park-ranger craft of helping visitors find meaning in a place, not just facts.
The international ride safety standard from ISO/TC 254, closely aligned with EN 13814.
The rate at which acceleration changes; sudden jerk makes muscles overshoot and heads whip.
A workplace where honest errors can be reported without punishment while reckless acts are still addressed.
Small deliberate movement in a scene, such as a flag or steam, that keeps a space feeling alive.
A themed zone of a park where architecture, sound, food and rides all describe one place and story.
Acreage reserved in a masterplan for future lands, gates or hotels.
Sideways force on a rider in a turn, reduced by banking the track.
Kevin Lynch's term for how easily people can form a mental map of a place.
The number of days or nights a visiting party spends at a resort.
Fruin's A-to-F grade of how much space each walking person has, used to judge path width.
The chain or cable slope that gives a coaster train its stored energy before the first drop.
Disney's paid line-skipping product, renamed from Genie+ on July 24, 2024, with pre-booking windows.
Linear induction motor: track coils that push a plain metal fin on the train by inducing currents in it.
A launch using linear induction motors along the track, first used on Flight of Fear in 1996.
The average number of people in a queue equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each spends there.
Adapting a ride or story for a new country by changing its meaning, characters and symbols, not just its language.
Any ticketed experience guests travel to, from theme parks to VR arenas, immersive art venues and pop-ups.
A park plan where lands are arranged around a ring path, often circling a lagoon.
Linear synchronous motor: track coils that push permanent magnets on the train to launch or brake it.
A change to a ride significant enough that the design standard applies to it as if it were new.
A small study model used to test a form before building it at full size.
A planning role that lays out lands, capacities, circulation and phasing for a whole park or resort.
The combined heat a person feels from surrounding surfaces and sun; shade lowers it even when air temperature does not change.
The average running time between stoppages of a ride.
The code term for the protected route out of a building or area, sized by occupancy under rules like NFPA 101.
A computer built to play or render very large video streams to many projectors in perfect sync.
The local weather of a small space, shaped by shade, wind, water and surfaces, which can differ from the regional forecast.
The amusement strip of a fair, named after the Midway Plaisance of the 1893 Chicago exposition.
Steering the audience's attention toward one thing so a change elsewhere goes unnoticed.
A thin curtain of water droplets used as a see-through projection surface in nighttime shows.
A collage of images, colours and samples that fixes the feel of a project in one glance.
Simulation that solves the equations of motion for linked bodies such as a train, its bogies, restraints and track.
The state of being carried into a story so fully that attention, imagery and emotion all focus on it.
A small speaker placed low and close to guests so sound stays local instead of carrying across a land.
A junction or gathering point where paths meet and guests make a navigation decision.
Methods such as ultrasonic or magnetic particle inspection that find cracks and thinning without damaging the part.
Checking metal parts for hidden cracks with methods such as ultrasound or magnetic particles that do not damage them.
A design that predictably changes behaviour while leaving every option open, such as a default or an ordering.
The point at which a part or controller is no longer made and must be reverse-engineered or redesigned.
Waiting time filled with something to look at or do, which feels shorter than empty time.
A continuous chain of swivelling ride vehicles that lets designers point every rider at each scene.
Speakers mounted in the ride vehicle so each rider hears a soundtrack that follows the ride.
Any part of the park a guest can see, hear or smell, which must belong to the story.
Disney's theatre metaphor for public areas versus hidden operational areas.
The hourly rider count a ride actually achieves after empty seats, slow loads and stoppages.
The utricle and saccule, inner-ear sensors for linear acceleration and head tilt.
A temporary change of props, lighting and audio that gives a ride a seasonal story without altering the hardware.
The surge of guests arriving at nearby rides the moment a parade or show ends.
A dated booking required to enter a park, adopted widely after the 2020 reopenings.
The look of age added with glazes or chemicals so a new surface reads as decades old.
The design requirement, in standards such as ASTM F2291, that a restraint and seat keep the rider safely in the vehicle through all ride forces.
We judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending rather than its average.
Fruin's A-to-F grading of walkways, stairs and queues by how much space each person has.
The area available per walking person, in square metres, the basic measure behind level of service.
An illusion in which a lit figure reflects in an angled sheet of glass so it appears as a transparent ghost on stage.
Revenue divided by attendance; the average amount each guest visit brings in.
Choosing the slice of a population, such as the 5th to 95th percentile, that a design must fit.
The ISO 13849 rating from a to e that expresses the reliability required of a safety-related control function.
A control-system condition, such as all restraints locked, that must be true before dispatch is allowed.
Universal Orlando's name for its opt-out face-matching entry and attraction check system.
A narrow spot where paths, queues or exits collide and the crowd slows or stalls.
Slater's term for the sense of being in a place, produced by consistent sensory input that responds to your movement.
Slater's term for the sense that events are really happening, produced by a world that reacts to you and behaves consistently.
A paid public garden of the 17th to 19th centuries offering music, lights, food and early rides.
Walt Disney's verb for improving something that already works by adding one more detail.
The queue time a park displays in its app or at the entrance, which third-party forecasters log and which often differs from the real wait.
The view that motion sickness follows prolonged failure to keep the body stable, not sensory mismatch.
A short, timed performance between the queue and the ride that sets up story and rules for a group.
Replacing or servicing a part when its sensor data shows wear beginning, rather than after failure or on a fixed calendar.
Inspecting and replacing parts on a schedule set by hours or cycles, before they fail.
Short for previsualization: a rough animated version of a ride or scene made to test timing and views.
A portfolio that shows sketches, options and decisions for each project, not only finished renders.
A production role that builds and maintains the project schedule across design, fabrication and installation.
Projecting video that has been warped and masked to fit a three-dimensional surface such as a face or a castle.
The body's sense of where its limbs are and how hard its muscles are working.
The idea that people prefer places where they can see out (prospect) while feeling sheltered (refuge).
A felt sense of safety, from trust in the ride or distance from the danger, that lets fear become fun.
Edward T. Hall's study of the personal-space distances people keep from one another.
Flames, flashes and sparks fired close to an audience, governed in the US by NFPA 1126.
An inductive sensor that detects a metal flag passing without contact, used to count cars.
A low-stimulation space with dim lighting and soft seating where an overloaded guest can recover inside the park.
The volume a rider's outstretched limbs could occupy, swept along the ride path, which must stay clear of structure.
Game-engine software that renders ride media frame by frame during the ride so it can react to riders and timing.
A second independent means of performing a critical safety function in case the first fails.
A planned closure in which a ride's trains, structure, controls or scenes are renewed.
Training a controller by trial and reward in simulation until it reliably performs a task, such as walking in character without falling.
The part of us that tells the story of an experience afterwards, as opposed to the part that lives it.
The tendency to recall more memories from roughly ages 10 to 30 than from other periods.
Leaving a queue after joining it, before being served.
Checking that each rider's bar or belt is closed and locked before dispatch; today manual, with camera-based patents filed.
A ticket handed out when a ride breaks down that lets the guest come back later without queueing.
The planned moment a hidden view suddenly opens up as a payoff.
Apter's idea that the same arousal is felt as anxiety or excitement depending on the frame you are in.
A US university competition in which teams design and build a working model attraction to a shared prompt over six months.
An engineer who designs the vehicle, track and drive systems and proves they stay inside force and clearance limits.
A procedure letting adults in a group take turns on a ride while one waits with a child who cannot ride.
The structured process of finding hazards, estimating how bad and how likely they are, and reducing them until acceptable.
Energy lost as a tyre squashes and recovers on the rail, a small fraction of the wheel load.
The morning rush when gates open and guests race to the most popular rides.
A plot of stress range against cycles to failure used to predict fatigue life.
An IEC 61508 rating from 1 to 4 that caps how often a safety function may fail dangerously.
A programmable controller with redundant, self-checking hardware rated for safety-critical functions.
TEA's signature conference on experience design, held regionally each year.
A replaceable cartridge soaked with fragrance that a scent machine blows air across to release the smell.
The phase that turns a concept into rough plans, elevations and sketches that fix size and layout.
Greenhouse gases from a company's own operations and from the electricity it buys; the basis of park climate targets.
The list of guest-facing elements a theming contractor must build, drawn to separate them from base building.
A loosely woven cloth that looks solid when lit from the front and transparent when the scene behind it is lit.
A temporary re-dressing of an attraction or land for a holiday, installed and removed on a yearly cycle.
A rough full-size mock-up of a ride seat used to test fit, reach and restraints with real people.
Three fluid-filled rings in each inner ear that detect head rotation.
A personality trait describing how strongly someone craves intense, novel and risky experiences.
The view that motion sickness comes from a mismatch between what the eyes, inner ear and body expect and report.
A published rating of each attraction on sound, light, smell, touch and motion so guests can plan around sensory needs.
A notice from a manufacturer or regulator telling all owners of a ride type about a fault or required check.
A pre-existing ride design exempted from a new design standard because its safe operating history is documented.
Bitner's term for the built environment of a service, covering ambient conditions, layout and signs, and how it shapes behaviour.
The objects, clutter and wear placed in a scene to make it look inhabited.
Concrete sprayed through a hose onto lath, then hand carved into rock texture.
The quieter weeks on either side of a park's peak, often filled with ticketed events.
Mechanised scenery such as moving walls, drops or boulders that is neither a vehicle nor a character figure.
The system that cues lights, audio, video, figures and effects so they run together on a timeline or from triggers.
A show technology role that writes the cue logic linking ride position to lights, audio, media, effects and figures.
The hybrid creative-and-management role that owns an attraction's creative content through design and installation.
A creative role that turns concept art into dimensioned plans, elevations and models of scenes that can be built.
The writer responsible for an attraction's story bible, scripts, signage copy and character voice.
A coaster layout that does not form a circuit; the train reverses and rides the same track backward.
An early coaster whose cars are guided by side wheels against boards rather than held down on the rail.
The straight line from a guest's eye to whatever is in view, which designers check for out-of-story objects.
Moving a controller trained in simulation onto physical hardware, usually helped by randomizing the simulator's physics.
The brain's habit of judging an object's size from assumed distance, which forced perspective exploits.
Disney's nickname for a fan-driven scent dispenser that pushes a chosen aroma into a scene or street on a schedule.
Helbing and Molnar's 1995 way of writing pedestrian motion as physics: a pull toward a goal plus pushes away from people and walls.
The tendency to copy what other people are doing when unsure, such as joining a line because it is long.
Adding deliberate sound so unwanted mechanical noise becomes less noticeable.
Theme-park slang for any spoken script, recorded or delivered live by an operator.
A water-filled trough at the end of a track section that slows a boat on a flume or water coaster.
The landing of a water-ride boat into a pool that stops it and throws up a wave.
Pre-distorting a 3D image so it looks correct from a moving ride vehicle's viewpoint rather than from a fixed seat.
An ASTM document that sets out an agreed way of doing something, such as designing or inspecting a ride.
A six-legged hexapod that moves a platform in all six degrees of freedom.
The shared reference document holding a fictional world's characters, history and rules.
Joe Rohde's term for a place built to be explored rather than a plot to be retold.
A monorail whose car wraps over the top of a single beam on rubber tyres.
A full-circuit coaster 400 ft or taller, begun by Top Thrill Dragster in 2003.
Disney Research's untethered stunt-double figure that flips in free flight and lands on its mark using onboard sensing.
Continuing to invest time or money because of what has already been spent rather than what lies ahead.
The railway term for banking: raising the outer rail of a curve so the force comes through the seat.
A fast stand-in, often a neural network trained on simulation output, that answers an engineering question in microseconds instead of minutes.
James Reason's picture of layered defences with holes; harm only passes when the holes line up.
A movable section of track that sends a train onto a different route mid-ride.
An 1880s gravity ride where a car coasted one way, was pushed to a second track, and coasted back.
The habit of tracing how one design change moves throughput, cost, pacing and safety before committing to it.
Deep ability in one craft plus working knowledge of the neighbouring disciplines, the profile themed entertainment teams hire for.
Deliberately choosing surfaces guests will touch so texture and temperature support the story and survive wear.
The Themed Entertainment Association, the trade body for the companies and people who design and build experiences.
TEA's programme for students and early-career professionals, including a six-month mentorship and discounted event entry.
A preview run with real guests, where the ride may close at any time, used to train staff and find faults.
The weeks after install when ride, show and operations are run and tuned before guests ride.
The Themed Entertainment Association's peer award for outstanding projects, given since 1994.
TEA's annual awards for outstanding achievement in themed entertainment, first presented in 1994.
The riders a ride could serve per hour if every seat were filled and every dispatch left on time.
Setup, confrontation and resolution, mapped onto queue, ride and exit.
A gate, tunnel or arch that signals the move from one story world into another.
Toronto Metropolitan University's invitational student design contest held around IAAPA Expo since 2014.
A park's published scale, from gentle to aggressive, telling guests how intense a ride is.
Leaning a simulator seat slowly so gravity imitates a sustained acceleration.
A running clock in hours, minutes, seconds and frames that every show device follows to stay in sync.
A card handed to a guest entering a queue and collected at the merge to measure the real wait.
A dark ride whose vehicles follow a programmed path across a floor using wire or positioning systems, not a track.
A battery-powered ride vehicle guided by floor markers or a buried wire instead of a rail.
A ride seat positioned and shaped so a guest can slide across to it from a wheelchair.
A sliding or rotating track section that moves trains onto a storage or maintenance siding.
The designed seam between two lands where music, paving and planting change over.
A length of track where curvature and bank ramp gradually between a straight and a curve.
A brake that slows a train to manage speed or forces but cannot stop it.
A picnic and amusement ground built by a streetcar company at the end of its line to sell weekend fares.
Track made from steel tubes that wheels grip on three sides, first used permanently on the Matterhorn in 1959.
Mori's observation that almost-human figures provoke unease rather than the affection given to clearly stylised ones.
A wheel that runs under the rail so a car cannot lift off, patented by John Miller in 1919.
Designing a space so the widest range of people can use it without special routes or exceptions.
A figure that carries its own power and computing so it can move without hoses or cables to the floor.
A wheel running under the rail that stops the train lifting off in inversions and over hills.
A utility corridor; at Magic Kingdom, the ground-level service tunnels the park was built on top of.
Demand divided by capacity; as it nears 100 percent, queues grow very quickly.
A spot where a slow train runs out of momentum and rolls back to the low point, stranding riders.
Reviewing a design to keep its function while cutting cost; in practice often just a budget cut.
The illusion of moving yourself when only the visual scene is moving.
The inner-ear sensors for rotation, linear acceleration and gravity.
Anything a guest can see that does not belong to the story, such as a plain show building or a crane.
Queasiness caused by moving images alone, such as in a dome or simulator theatre.
A roller coaster ridden with a headset whose film is synced to train speed and position; first at Europa-Park in 2015.
An attraction with no vehicle, where guests move through story rooms at their own pace.
Drifting a motion platform back to centre slower than riders can feel, so it is ready for the next cue.
Walt Disney's private design company of 1952, renamed Walt Disney Imagineering in 1986.
Walt Disney's word for a tall visual magnet, such as a castle, that pulls guests through a space and anchors their sense of direction.
The inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance or enjoyment: too little bores, too much overwhelms.
